teaser: The tower was due to be torn down. Delaunay painted it as if it were already shaking.

lesson.text: Stand on the Champ de Mars in Paris around 1910 and tip your head back. Above you rise 300 meters (about 985 feet) of bolted iron, then the tallest structure on Earth. It had been built for the World's Fair of 1889 with permission to stand for twenty years. The twenty years were up.

Robert Delaunay was four years old when the tower opened. He grew up with it on the skyline, and from 1909 he painted it again and again, more than a dozen times in three years. No old master had ever painted such a thing. That was exactly why he wanted it.

The tower survived its deadline partly because it was useful. Its top made a superb antenna for the new wireless telegraph, and the army wanted to keep it. A monument to engineering was saved by engineering.

His problem was simple to state. The tower is too tall to see in one go. Close to it, your eyes climb, drop, swing sideways. You never get the neat postcard outline. So Delaunay painted the climbing, dropping and swinging instead of the outline.

lesson.title: Bottom to top
lesson.text: The whole tower is here, but in pieces. Follow it the way your eyes would on the spot.

spots.title: The great arch
spots.text: You are almost underneath it. The dark iron arch between the legs curves over a patch of pale sky, crossed by thin struts.

spots.title: The first platform
spots.text: A tilted band with a row of little arcades: the first-floor gallery. It leans as if the deck were sliding to the right.

spots.title: The upper shaft
spots.text: Higher up, the tower turns orange and splits into slanting blades with a ladder of crossbars. This part is seen from farther away than the arch.

spots.title: The leaves
spots.text: Feathery leaves hang in from the left. The trees of the park act like a curtain you look through, and they bend with the same curves as the iron.

lesson.text: Did you feel the jump between the arch and the shaft? The arch is seen from below, the top from a distance, the platform from the side. Several viewpoints are stitched into one canvas. This idea came from Cubism, the Paris movement that broke objects into facets (small flat planes) to show more than one side at once.

Picasso and Braque applied it to quiet things: a guitar, a bottle, a seated friend. Delaunay turned it on a 300-meter machine in the open air. The result does not sit still like their pictures. It lurches.
Delaunay did not paint what the Eiffel Tower looks like. He painted what it is like to look at it: a string of glances that refuse to add up to one view.
Three kinds of movement hold this turbulence together.

lines.label: The arch
lines.text: A firm half circle anchors the bottom of the picture. Everything above it is less stable.

lines.label: The slipping deck
lines.text: The platform should be level. Delaunay tips it downhill to the right, and the tower above it seems to twist on its base.

lines.label: The sweep
lines.text: A long gray curve swings over the tower like a bent branch. Nature and iron share one rhythm.

lesson.text: The colors are held back: ochre, gray, a rusty orange for the iron, cream for the clouds. Look at the right side and you will see those clouds as stacks of round puffs, climbing in step with the tower. Even the air has been cut into units.

The painter trained in no art academy. As a teenager he was apprenticed to a workshop that painted theater scenery, where he learned to cover very large surfaces fast and to think of a picture as something seen from far away.

He later described these years as his “destructive” period. The word fits. Old ways of building a picture, with one fixed viewpoint and one steady horizon, are being pulled apart here, and the tower takes the damage.
Somewhere at the foot of all this iron stands an ordinary little house, a plain cube with a dark doorway. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The little house
spots.text: A pale box with a dark opening, tucked under the right leg next to a palm-like plant. It gives the scale: old Paris, tiny and calm, beside the giant.

lesson.text: That small house matters more than its size suggests. It is the only thing in the picture that keeps its shape. Around it the modern world bends and splinters. Delaunay was fascinated by that new world, but he does not pretend it is comfortable.

The tower was also a love token. Delaunay gave his first painting of it, made in 1909, to Sonia Terk, the Ukrainian-born artist he married the following year. She became a major painter of color in her own right.

The tower pictures traveled quickly. Shown in Paris and then in Munich with the Blue Rider group around Kandinsky, they made Delaunay better known in Germany than at home. One of them, bought by a Berlin collector, burned in the bombing of 1945.

Within two years he had stopped breaking things and started building with pure color. The tower stayed with him, though. It appears in his work into the 1920s, upright again, seen from the air, glowing red. The demolition order never came, for the tower or for his obsession.

quiz.question: Why could the Eiffel Tower have disappeared around 1909?
options: It was damaged by a storm
Its permit to stand ran for only twenty years
quiz.explanation: It was built for the 1889 World's Fair with permission to stand twenty years.

quiz.question: What did Delaunay borrow from Cubism?
options: Showing several viewpoints in one picture
quiz.explanation: The arch, platform and shaft are each seen from a different position.

quiz.question: Where did Delaunay learn his trade as a teenager?
options: At the Paris fine arts academy
In a workshop painting theater scenery
quiz.explanation: He was apprenticed to a theater scenery workshop and never attended an academy.

quiz.question: What is the one object in the picture that keeps a calm, regular shape?
options: The small house at the lower right
quiz.explanation: The little cube house stays intact while the tower around it bends.

quiz.question: What word did Delaunay later use for this period of his work?
quiz.explanation: He called it his destructive period, when the single fixed viewpoint was taken apart.

facts.text: Delaunay painted the Eiffel Tower only once.
facts.explanation: He painted it more than a dozen times between 1909 and 1912, and returned to it in the 1920s.

facts.text: The tower's use as a wireless antenna helped save it from demolition.
facts.explanation: Its height made it valuable for the new wireless telegraph.

facts.text: In this painting the first platform is drawn perfectly level.
facts.explanation: Delaunay tilts it down to the right, so the tower seems to twist.
